stories.teaser: A mother’s volunteer network now helps Israelis in trouble in 49 countries
stories.headline: Friends Rescuing Friends: a volunteer network founded by a bereaved mother now helps Israelis in emergencies in 49 countries
stories.why: More than 230 real emergencies handled since March 2023, free of charge to families.
texts:
“We built the rescue network to give others what we didn’t have at the time,” says Nirit Rimon.

After her son Yanai drowned in a river in Mexico in 2021, she founded Haverim Mehalzim (Friends Rescuing Friends), a volunteer network that helps Israelis and Jews facing emergencies abroad. Since March 2023 it has handled more than 230 real emergencies in 49 countries, free of charge to families.

#Israel #Volunteers #Rescue #SocialImpact

More than 1,000 requests. Over 230 real emergencies. 49 countries.

That’s the record so far of Friends Rescuing Friends, an Israeli volunteer network run under the nonprofit Gvanim. Its co-CEO Ron Lavi estimates that about 35 of those cases would likely have ended in death without the network’s help. Families pay nothing.

#Israel #Volunteers #Rescue #SocialImpact

What if help were already nearby wherever you traveled?

Friends Rescuing Friends started as a WhatsApp group. Now volunteers around the world are alerted by country, a coordination center manages information, a forward team works on the ground with local rescue services, and lawyers and psychologists support families.

An idea any community could borrow.

#Israel #Volunteers #Rescue #SocialImpact
stories.og_title: 'Is he a Mossad agent?': Inside Israel's global volunteer rescue network

stories.teaser: Technion physicists steer electrons with light in 860 attoseconds
stories.headline: Technion physicists use shaped laser light to steer electron currents in bursts of 860 attoseconds
stories.why: Published in Nature Photonics; works at room temperature and in air.
texts:
Steering electrons with light.

Technion physicists led by Prof. Michael Kruger shaped two-color infrared laser pulses to control which way electrons flow between a microscope’s nanometric tip and a sample. The current bursts lasted just 860 attoseconds. Published in Nature Photonics.

“Finally we managed to prove beyond any doubt that we are able to control the direction of the current.”

#Israel #Technion #Physics #Science

860 attoseconds.

That’s how long the electron current bursts lasted in a new Technion experiment, published in Nature Photonics. Using a scanning tunneling microscope and shaped laser pulses, the team controlled the direction of electron flow with a resolution of about 2 nanometers, at room temperature and in air, without a vacuum.

#Israel #Technion #Physics #Science

Can light act as a switch for electricity?

At the Technion, Prof. Michael Kruger’s team showed it can steer electron currents in either direction, in bursts lasting 860 attoseconds. It took several years and three different laser systems.

“We tested three different laser systems, and rebuilt the optical setup many times,” says Dr. Adi Goldner.

#Israel #Technion #Physics #Science

stories.teaser: Did early humans collect souvenirs half a million years ago?
stories.headline: Tel Aviv University researchers suggest early humans in Israel kept souvenirs half a million years ago
stories.why: Published in Evolutionary Anthropology, based on finds from Qesem Cave, Revadim, Jaljulia and Sechin Valley.
texts:
The first keepsakes?

Tel Aviv University researchers suggest that early humans in what is now Israel may have collected personal souvenirs as far back as half a million years ago: small colorful pebbles at Qesem Cave, hand axes shaped around fossils, and old weathered flint tools kept rather than discarded. Published in Evolutionary Anthropology.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Archaeology #Prehistory

Half a million years ago, people may already have been holding on to memories.

A Tel Aviv University team spanning zoology, archaeology and psychology, including Dr. Yoav Ram and Prof. Ran Barkai, proposes that special objects found at Israeli prehistoric sites served as souvenirs, and may have shaped the evolution of autobiographical memory. The authors stress it is a hypothesis.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Archaeology #Prehistory

“An object like this may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives,” says Dr. Yoav Ram of Tel Aviv University.

The team looked at colorful pebbles, fossil-decorated hand axes and reused old flint tools from Qesem Cave and other Israeli sites, and suggests early humans kept them as keepsakes.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Archaeology #Prehistory

stories.teaser: Israeli-American AI that helps prevent blindness wins the Prix Galien
stories.headline: Israeli-American AEYE Health wins the Prix Galien USA award for AI that screens for diabetic eye disease
stories.why: Its FDA-cleared AEYE-DS gives near-immediate eye exam results without a physician reading the images.
texts:
AI that helps prevent blindness, now award-winning.

Israeli-American company AEYE Health won the 2026 Prix Galien USA Award for Best Digital Health Solution. Its FDA-cleared AEYE-DS performs diabetic eye exams autonomously, with portable or tabletop retinal cameras, giving near-immediate results without a physician interpreting the images. It was validated in three phase-III clinical trials.

#Israel #AI #HealthTech #Diabetes

Three phase-III clinical trials. FDA clearance. And now the Prix Galien.

AEYE Health’s AEYE-DS, invented by co-founder and CEO Dr. Zack Dvey-Aharon, was named Best Digital Health Solution at the 2026 Prix Galien USA Awards in New York. The fully autonomous AI screens for diabetic eye disease at virtually any point of care.

#Israel #AI #HealthTech #Diabetes

What if a diabetic eye exam didn’t need a specialist on hand?

That’s what AEYE-DS does, delivering results in moments from a retinal photo. The Israeli-American innovation just won the Prix Galien USA Award for Best Digital Health Solution.

“We are only at the beginning of what autonomous AI can accomplish for global healthcare,” says Dr. Zack Dvey-Aharon.

#Israel #AI #HealthTech #Diabetes
stories.og_title: Israeli-American AEYE Health wins Prix Galien Award for new AI technology helping prevent blindness
